task: For this synthetic writing exercise, use the fictional reporting notes to write a reported feature for a general newspaper audience. Write from this reporting snapshot as of April 9, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Hartwell Works is a city-supported retraining program for former employees of the closed Keystone Motors assembly plant. Its April 2025 report supplies the enrollment, completion, employment and wage figures in these notes.
Keystone Motors closed the Hartwell plant on December 31, 2021, eliminating 2,800 direct jobs; economists estimated the closure cost the region an additional 1,400 supplier and service jobs.
Hartwell, a fictional city of approximately 43,000 residents in western Michigan, had built its economy around the plant for more than five decades.

The Hartwell Works program, a partnership among Hartwell Community College, fictional technology manufacturer Vertex Systems, and precision manufacturer Clearline Manufacturing, began accepting enrollees in March 2022.
By April 2025, approximately 1,100 of the plant's former workers had enrolled in Hartwell Works; 780 had completed a certification program — a completion rate of 71 percent.
Of the 780 certification completers, 499 found relevant employment within six months, approximately 64 percent.
The program has cost approximately $14.2 million, financed through Michigan Department of Labor and federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act grants.
The average hourly wage in jobs obtained by Hartwell Works completers is $22.50; the average hourly wage at Keystone Motors before closure was $28.40 — a difference of $5.90 per hour.
Hartwell Mayor Sandra Alvarado said: "Sixty-four percent would be a good graduation rate at a lot of colleges. For a workforce-crisis response, I do not know if it is enough."
James Petrov, 52, worked at Keystone for 19 years, earning $31 an hour; he completed the Hartwell Works CNC operator track in 2023 and was hired at Clearline Manufacturing at $23 an hour.
Petrov said: "I am working. My house is paid for. But I will not make what I made at Keystone again."

Among Hartwell Works enrollees, 40 percent were over 50. Among certification completers over 50, the six-month relevant-employment rate was 51 percent, compared with approximately 64 percent among all completers.

Approximately 1,700 of the plant's 2,800 former workers did not enroll in Hartwell Works. Administrators estimate that about 400 of these non-enrollees left the Hartwell area, about 300 retired early, and the remaining approximately 1,000 are unemployed or in part-time work.

The information technology and computer-skills training tracks had a completion rate of 38 percent, compared with the program's overall 71 percent; administrators attributed the gap to the prior-skills deficit for workers with no computer background.
The 65-acre former Keystone plant site was demolished in 2023 and has been listed for sale at $8.5 million; it has attracted no buyers in 18 months.
Hartwell's combined property and income tax revenue fell 19 percent between 2021 and 2024, straining street maintenance and the fire department.
The manufacturing training tracks — CNC machining, industrial electrical, and welding — produced an 83 percent completion rate and a 72 percent placement rate.
Vertex Systems has hired 64 Hartwell Works completers; a Vertex spokeswoman described the arrangement as "mutually beneficial" but declined to say whether it offered wages comparable to Keystone.
The Michigan Department of Labor said Hartwell Works had the highest per-enrollee completion rate of any plant-closure response program it had funded in the past decade.
Alvarado said the city had applied for a federal Economic Adjustment Assistance grant to fund a three-year study of the Hartwell Works model and publish a replication guide for other communities.
Petrov said he had encouraged two former colleagues to enroll in the program, but both declined. He said of one: "He was 58. He told me the math didn't work. I don't think he was wrong."

The Hartwell Works program has been renewed for an additional two years with continued state funding; program director Carmen Ruiz expects to enroll an additional 200 workers from other industries facing layoffs.
